vignette:
She is a 28-year-old European woman who works as a teacher and comes to describe a life that changed gradually, then all at once, after she realizes she is being stalked by a former acquaintance. At first, the contact feels merely inconvenient: repeated messages, unexpected appearances, a string of "coincidental" encounters that leave her uneasy but unsure whether she is overreacting. She tries to dismiss her discomfort and tells herself that being polite, being reasonable, and keeping the peace will make the problem fade. Instead, the attention intensifies. He learns her routines, notices where she parks, comments on things she has not told him directly, and appears to know details about her day that he should not know. The sense of being watched begins to seep into everything.

For a while, she keeps functioning. She teaches classes, grades papers at night, and maintains the careful composure expected of her in front of students, colleagues, and her partner. But the stalking gradually changes the texture of ordinary life. She begins checking over her shoulder in the grocery store, on the walk to her car, outside her apartment building. She changes routes without deciding to, then feels foolish for doing so. She starts to scan faces automatically, trying to determine whether someone nearby is simply another pedestrian or someone waiting for her. When her phone lights up, her body tightens before she has even read the message. She describes a constant low-level alertness, as if her mind no longer allows her to fully rest.

As the intrusions continue, sleep becomes difficult. She lies awake replaying conversations, wondering whether she missed a warning sign or said something that encouraged him. When she does fall asleep, she wakes quickly and disoriented, listening for sounds in the hallway or outside her window. She checks locks more than once, sometimes several times before bed, and feels compelled to look out curtains she has already closed. She keeps the lights on longer in the evening than she used to. Even at school, where she is usually most herself, she notices herself positioning her desk so she can see the door. She feels embarrassed by how hard it is to focus on lesson plans or student questions when part of her attention is always tracking the room.

Her relationship becomes both a refuge and a source of guilt. Her partner wants to help, but she struggles to explain why she cannot simply "move on." She does not want to burden him with the details and sometimes minimizes what is happening, then feels isolated when she cannot accept comfort. She becomes irritable when he asks whether she has reported another message or whether she has been outside alone. At times she sounds angry with him, though the anger is often a cover for fear. She also notices a painful shift in how she sees herself: once confident and competent, she now feels fragile, exposed, and ashamed that someone else's fixation has made her question her own judgment.

She avoids places that once felt ordinary. She takes less interest in after-work errands, declines invitations that would require her to stay out late, and stops lingering near her car at school. If she sees a figure who resembles him, her stomach drops and her mind goes blank for a moment, as if her body is already reacting before she has time to think. She describes intrusive memories of specific moments-an unexpected appearance, a message that made her skin crawl, the feeling of being followed down a street-returning without invitation, accompanied by nausea and a racing heart. She becomes distressed by the smallest reminders: a notification sound, a certain route home, a car that circles more than once.

Over time, the stalking has not only frightened her; it has changed her sense of safety in her own life. She remains committed to her students and is often praised for being careful, organized, and present in the classroom, but maintaining that surface takes much more effort now. Beneath it is a woman who is constantly trying to anticipate danger, who feels watched even when no one is there, and who measures her days by how exposed she may be.
